claims.text: Wear performance of high-entropy-alloy protective coatings is primarily governed by the formation and stability of a dynamically oxidized surface oxide layer.
A wear-generated oxide layer enriched in elements such as Cr or Al is self-lubricating.
The dynamically formed oxide layer reduces friction and protects the underlying coating.
Reducing oxidation-facilitating elements impairs protective oxide-layer formation and degrades wear resistance.
The baseline coating has a homogeneous multicomponent microstructure and is known to form a stable oxide layer during wear.
The concentration of a selected oxidation-facilitating element, such as Cr, will be reduced by about 10–20% relative to the baseline.
Ambient-air wear testing from room temperature to approximately 300°C can promote dynamic oxidation without melting or extreme thermal degradation.
A continuous surface oxide layer enriched in the selected critical element acts as both a solid lubricant and a barrier against wear.
Preferential oxidation of the critical alloying element during wear produces the self-lubricating oxide film.
Reducing the critical element concentration makes the oxide layer less robust.
A less robust oxide layer causes higher friction and increased wear.
The baseline coating will form a more robust and continuous oxide layer than the reduced-element coating.
The baseline coating will have lower wear rates and coefficients of friction than the reduced-element coating.
The reduced-element coating will exhibit a thinner or more discontinuous oxide layer.
The proposed mechanism should hold for chemically similar high-entropy coatings when dynamic oxidation is the dominant wear-mediating process.
The proposed mechanism may not apply under inert conditions or at temperatures that prevent oxide formation.
Interactions among alloying elements and nonlinear oxide-film formation kinetics may alter the quantitative wear response to reducing the selected element.
Failure of the reduced-element coating to show either a significant wear-rate increase or a notably poorer oxide layer relative to the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
